extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_short: patent infringement defenses and injunction practice
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of substantive defenses to patent infringement (prior use/sale, abandonment/dedication, priority, fraud, alien withholding, surrender/reissue) and equitable remedies (injunction principles, parties entitled, court discretion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior purchase, sale, or public use before application
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchase, sale, or prior use before the application for a patent shall not invalidate it, unless it amounts to an abandonment to the public; such acts do not per se invalidate, but if connected with facts showing abandonment to the public, or if they occurred more than two years prior to the application, they will invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and case law (e.g., McClurg v. Kingsland) show that short uses with patentee's consent or within employment may justify a presumption of license rather than abandonment. The statute's two-year rule creates a temporal forfeiture: use or sale more than two years before application works a forfeiture of the right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of 'newly invented machine, manufacture, or composition of matter' phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute's phrase 'newly invented machine, manufacture, or composition of matter' is to be construed to mean 'the invention patented,' i.e., whatever may be the subject-matter of a valid patent, including processes or methods of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court construction treats 'the specific machine' as referring to the thing as originally invented and protects the particular invention patented rather than limiting protection to literal 'machine' forms. This avoids making statutory protection depend on mere phraseology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment/dedication to the public requires proof beyond isolated acts
rubrics_metrics.description: An abandonment to the public will not be proved by the particular act of use or sale alone; the act of use or sale may be attended with circumstances amounting to abandonment, and abandonment may also be proved by other acts or omissions disconnected from the particular use or sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must show circumstances indicating a dedication to the public (e.g., long open use, lack of notices, conduct of the patentee). Courts look to connected facts and may consider other acts/omissions by the patentee in assessing abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-year safe period for inventor's commercial use
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor may make and use his machines and vend and take pay for them for two years previous to his application without forfeiting patent benefits; but selling, using, or putting into public use more than two years before application forfeits the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise explains this as virtually extending the patentee's practical privilege for sixteen years (including pre-application commercial exploitation for two years) but strictly bars uses beyond that two-year window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of purchasers/constructors with inventor's knowledge or consent prior to application
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who purchased of the inventor, or with his knowledge and consent constructed any newly invented or discovered machine or other patentable article prior to the inventor's application, or sold or used one so constructed, shall have the right to use and vend to others the specific thing so made or purchased without liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory protection allows those who acquired/constructed the specific article with inventor's consent to continue use of that specific thing; protection is to the 'specific thing' made or purchased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing/specification does not automatically dedicate described parts to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: A description in an applicant's specification of a machine or part, unaccompanied by notice that he has rights in it or desires to secure title, is not necessarily a dedication to the public; the patentee may surrender and amend specification or claim to cure defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Battin v. Taggert reversed lower-court instruction that description alone is dedication. Reissue and amended specifications under statutory remedies can validate claims within the scope of the original invention; surrender/reissue remedies limit what passes to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender and reissue effects on rights and suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A surrender of the patent to the commissioner that extinguishes the patent (legal cancellation) prevents reliance on that patent after the surrender; reissue affects subsequent suits but not antecedent suits which depend on the patent's existence at commencement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat surrender as extinguishing the original title; reissued patents must be for the same invention substantially and cannot claim a new and different invention. Monetary recoveries under the original patent are not automatically recoverable upon surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense for surreptitious or unjust obtaining of a patent (fraud on true inventor)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee surreptitiously or unjustly obtained the patent for that which was in fact invented or discovered by another who was using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting the same, that is a statutory defense and a complete bar to an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This embraces both outright fraud where a non-inventor obtains a patent and the case where two independent inventors exist and the later applicant succeeds despite the earlier inventor's diligence; courts examine records and the conduct/diligence of the claimed first inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of knowledge from public records and inference of piracy
rubrics_metrics.description: When an inventor has filed a description or obtained a patent and recorded specifications/drawings, every subsequent applicant is presumed to have knowledge of the preceding record; a jury may infer piracy from existence of the prior record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption supports an inference of copying where later patentees obtain patents for similar machines; equitable principles about notice from documents are applied to patent applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority among independent inventors qualified by reasonable diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: In a contest between two independent inventors, one who first actually perfected and adapted the invention to use is entitled to the patent, but the statute qualifies that right by giving a prior right to the first inventor if he is using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imperfect, theoretical, or un-reduced-to-practice inventions are not patentable; 'reasonable diligence' in developing the invention is the key metric for awarding priority to an earlier inventor who has not yet perfected the device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien patentee's duty to put invention on sale (18-month clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee was an alien when the patent was granted and failed to put and continue on sale to the public, on reasonable terms, the invention for which the patent was issued for eighteen months from the date of the patent, that failure is a statutory defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was designed to prevent foreigners from obtaining patents in the U.S. and withholding use of their inventions from the public unreasonably; courts have interpreted its application in particular contexts (e.g., exceptions for American patentees as assignees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable grounds for injunctions in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The grounds of equity jurisdiction to grant injunctions in patent cases include prevention of irreparable mischief, suppression of multiplicity of suits and vexatious litigation, and more complete discovery from an infringer of the extent of injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute authorizes courts to grant injunctions 'according to the course and principles of courts of equity' and to impose 'terms and conditions' as reasonable. Courts apply established equitable rules when deciding injunctive relief in patent disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion and options in granting interlocutory and final injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The court has wide but regulated discretion when an interlocutory injunction is sought: it may grant an injunction at once; grant subject to the plaintiff establishing title at law or suspend until legal investigation with accounting by defendant; or dismiss. At hearing it may grant without a law trial if justice requires, retain the bill to allow action at law, or dismiss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision depends on conduct and dealings of parties, frame of pleadings, nature of patent right, and the evidence. Precedent (e.g., Lord Cottenham's remarks) outlines these courses and indicates they must be applied reasonably to case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties entitled to equitable relief and necessary joinder rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person holding the legal title or the right to bring an action (patentee, assignees, grantees of exclusive rights) may bring a bill for an injunction; an assignee with the whole interest may sue alone, but if the assignee has less than the whole interest he must join the patentee. An unrecorded assignment does not substitute the assignee to the rights/responsibilities necessary to maintain suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules governing who must be a party mirror those in actions at law; recording status affects standing. Where disclaimer or joiner issues exist, the proper parties must be before the court to obtain equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence or laches can defeat equitable injunctive relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiescence in open infringements or laches by the patentee may be sufficient grounds in equity for refusing an injunction even if a court of law might provide other remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Wyeth v. Stone) indicates that equitable relief can be denied where the patentee has for some time acquiesced in public infringements; equity focuses on fairness and delay when exercising its discretion.
